Subject: Retention & redaction options for PHI in Redwood

Hi Aditya —

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. As we dig into procurement, our security team has two priority asks before we can move a template PO: (1) firm guidance on retention limits for PHI-derived tokens/logs and (2) practical redaction approaches we can implement without sacrificing model quality for our triage workflows.

Attached is a short list of our use cases and minimal compliance expectations. High level questions we need answered for our legal & security review:
- Can Redwood enforce a per-customer retention window for raw request/response logs (e.g., 30/90/365 days) that is automatically purged?
- Does Redwood support configurable redaction at ingestion (PII stripping) vs. post-processing? Pros/cons?
- For scenarios where we must retain telemetry for troubleshooting, can we store only pseudonymized vectors/embeddings rather than plaintext?
- What are the operational controls (audit logs, KMS, export/delete APIs) around deletion requests?

Could you send a brief written Q&A and any matrix you have that maps options -> tradeoffs? We need something we can pass to procurement by EOD Friday.

Thanks,
Sara
Sara Long
Director, IT Security
St. Martin Health

Hi Sara —

Appreciate the clear list. Looping in Monica from Customer Success so we can turn this into a one-page decision matrix and an implementation plan. Technical details below come from Karthik on our side — we should be able to give you the short Q&A + matrix by tomorrow.

Immediate answers (short):
- Retention windows: yes — per-customer retention policies are configurable and enforced by automated purge jobs. Typical buckets: 30/90/365 days; custom values possible on Dedicated/Private plans.
- Redaction at ingestion vs post-processing: supported both ways. Ingestion redaction reduces data sent to models but may require you to surface enough context for correct outputs. Post-processing allows full model context but requires robust scrubbing of outputs before storage.
- Embeddings/pseudonymization: we can store only embeddings and a reversible mapping kept in your KMS if you choose; we also support one-way pseudonymization when irreversibility is required.
- Deletion controls: API-driven deletion, admin console erasure workflows, audit trail of delete events, and support ticket prioritization for emergency erasure.

Next steps: Monica will propose a short matrix and recommend which approach maps to each of your listed use cases. Karthik, can you add the technical pros/cons and the suggested default config for a healthcare triage workload?

Regards,

Folks — forwarding a compact technical brief below you can pass to Sara. Attaching the redaction matrix as well.

(Attachment: redaction-matrix.xlsx)

Technical Q&A / tradeoffs (healthcare triage focus):

1) Retention enforcement
- Implementation: retention is enforced at the storage tier with metadata-tagging per-tenant. A scheduled purge job deletes raw request/response blobs and associated KV cache entries after the configured TTL.
- Guarantees: for Dedicated/Private we perform physical deletions; for hosted plans we mark and scrub data from hot storage and remove keys from encrypted archives. We provide deletion proofs (audit logs + timestamps).

2) Redaction strategies
- Ingestion redaction (best-effort): regex/token-based PII scrubbing at the edge. Pros: minimizes exposure to models; faster compliance. Cons: can remove clinical identifiers that are necessary for context -> risk of reduced model accuracy. Works well for structured fields (MRN, SSN, DOB).
- Pseudonymization (recommended for mid-term): replace identifiers with reversible tokens stored in your KMS-protected mapping or a customer-managed secret. Pros: preserves context for models. Cons: requires secure mapping storage and policies for re-identification.
- Output filtering + redact-on-write: keep full transcript for model, apply ML-powered PII detectors before any write to storage. Pros: highest model fidelity; Cons: requires robust classifier and auditing to avoid leakage.

3) Embeddings/Telemetry storage
- Option A: store only embeddings (one-way). Embeddings are non-reversible by default but can leak semantic info; for highest safety store hashed/pseudonymized keys and rotate salts.
- Option B: reversible pseudonymization with mapping under your KMS — good for analytics traceability.

4) KV cache and session data
- Configurable TTL per model/session. For triage low-latency sessions we recommend short KV TTL (30m–2h) and explicit session closure to flush caches.

5) Operational controls
- Deletion API: immediate purge endpoints (sync or async depending on size).
- Audit evidence: immutable logs for delete requests, with signer, timestamp, and storage keys removed.
- Key management: support for customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault), HSM for on-prem.

6) Regulatory guidance
- For short retention (30 days): ingestion redaction + delete raw transcripts.
- For required audit trails (365 days): pseudonymize before storage, store audit-only keys under customer KMS, provide restricted engineer access and read-only exports for regulators.

7) Emergency erase / legal hold
- We support legal holds that suspend purge jobs; removal is reversible only with holder authorization. For erasure requests we provide erasure confirmations and cross-checks in audit logs.

Suggested default config for St. Martin triage pilot:
- Ingestion: enable token-based scrubbers for structured PHI fields + ML detector for free text;
- Storage: store transient raw transcripts for 7 days, keep pseudonymized embeddings for 180 days;
- KV TTL: 1 hour per session;
- Keys: customer-managed KMS;
- Ops: enable delete API + weekly purge report to your security mailbox.

I'll attach a short one-page summary (redaction-options-overview.pdf) you can hand to legal. If they need a dataflow diagram or sample deletion proof, we can produce both.
